MultiInstance

General Concept: A MultiInstance marker in BPMN allows an activity or subprocess to be repeated multiple times, either sequentially or in parallel. It is used for batch processing, approvals, or any scenario where the same logic must be applied to multiple items.

 

TaktX Implementation: In TaktX, MultiInstance wraps the target activity or subprocess and manages its repeated execution. Loop characteristics are defined using FEEL expressions. Each instance has its own variable scope, and results can be aggregated. MultiInstance supports both sequential and parallel execution, and can be combined with input/output mappings and error handling.

Usage & Options in TaktX:
A MultiInstance (loop) in TaktX allows you to:

  • Repeat execution of an activity or subprocess for each item in a collection.
  • Choose sequential or parallel execution for performance and control. Note: Even in parallel mode, the process always waits for all instances to complete before continuing.
  • Define input/output mappings and aggregate results from all instances.
  • Configure error handling, retries, and compensation for each instance.
  • Monitor execution and audit results for all instances via the TaktX client.
  • Use for batch processing, parallel workflows, or iterative logic.

 

Example: Multi-Stage Review with MultiInstance Subprocess

 

This example shows a process where a MultiInstance subprocess is used for reviewing multiple applications in parallel. Each application is reviewed, and based on the outcome, may require a manual check. Applications can be approved or rejected. The process continues only after all reviews are complete. This demonstrates advanced batch processing, conditional logic, and parallel execution in TaktX.

Tips & Tricks:

  • Use inputCollection to drive batch processing or approvals.
  • Use loopCnt for custom logic or to track progress.
  • Aggregate results with outputCollection for downstream processing.
  • Document mappings and expected results for maintainability.

Pitfalls:

  • Large parallel loops can impact performance.
  • Unmapped variables will not be available in each instance.
  • Uncaught errors can terminate all instances.
